title: Non-compete clauses in employment contracts
summary: About one in five Australian workers is bound by a non-compete clause, including many in lower-paid jobs. The clauses stop workers moving to rivals or starting their own firms. A ban below an income threshold is proposed from 2027 (see the related reform).
direction_rationale: Restraints stop workers moving to the employers who value them most and stop them starting competing firms, which lowers wages and slows the spread of know-how.

verified.notes: A business practice, not a law: no dates. The one-in-five share is the ABS figure (2024) cited by the Productivity Commission and Treasury.

review.notes: Drafted by AI-assisted desk research on 28 October 2026 (phase 4 of the productivity framework pivot) from the sources cited. Not yet checked by a person: verify the description, industries and assessment before use.

assessment.summary: Non-compete clauses bind about one in five workers. They keep people from moving to better-paid jobs with rivals or starting their own firms: one of the clearest barriers to labour mobility in Australia.

marks.reason: Restraints keep a large share of the workforce from moving to rivals.
Workers cannot leave to start competing firms.

assessment.confidence_note: The Productivity Commission modelled a 0.10 to 0.19% rise in GDP from reform.
